claims.statement: `plugin.json` is the only file the host looks for inside a plugin directory, and the two failure policies differ: a missing or invalid required field (`id`, `name`, `version`, `entry`) rejects the whole manifest so the plugin is never installed, while a bad optional field (unknown `capabilities` entries, non-numeric `order`, non-string `mount`) is dropped and the manifest survives; `readManifest` folds a missing file and unparsable JSON into the same error shape as a validation failure.

Manifest validation is also addressing validation: `id` must match the lowercase hostname charset /^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9._-]*$/ because it doubles as the `deck-plugin://` host name, and `entry` must be a `.js`/`.mjs` path inside the plugin directory — absolute paths, drive letters, backslashes, non-module extensions and any `..` segment are rejected before the plugin can be installed.

`PluginHostService` is a cordis `Service` registered as `plugins` that performs its first scan synchronously in its constructor — so the first `PanelSnapshot.plugins` section is already populated — and registers both the directory watchdog and a dispose handler on the context.

Each installed plugin is represented by a `PluginInstance` carrying its `PluginInfo`, manifest and directory plus a cordis-subset lifecycle of `ready(ctx)`/`dispose()`; the default factory implements both hooks as empty no-ops because today's desktop components render in the page and own no main-process resource, so the hooks are contract positions rather than behaviour.

`rescan()` diffs per-id asset fingerprints and acts on the difference: a new id is installed with `revision = 1`, a changed fingerprint unloads the old instance, bumps `revision` and installs again (that is the reload path), a vanished id is unloaded and its generation record dropped, and the rebuilt listing is sorted by `order` then id and emitted as `plugins/changed` only when its serialized form actually changed.

The asset fingerprint covers the serialized manifest plus only the entry module's `mtimeMs:size` (`missing` when absent), which means editing another file in the same plugin directory triggers a rescan from the watcher but produces no generation change: a reload requires touching `plugin.json` or the entry module.

Scanning is deliberately two-pass so a valid manifest always outranks a broken directory for an id: pass 1 lets valid manifests claim their ids in root order with the first root winning duplicate ids, and pass 2 admits directories whose `plugin.json` is missing or invalid under a sanitized directory-derived fallback id only when that id is still free; because production passes the built-in cards root first, a user plugin can never displace a built-in id.

A broken plugin is listed rather than silently dropped: an invalid manifest produces no instance at all but appears in the listing as `status: 'error'` with `entry: ''`, and a valid manifest whose entry asset is missing is likewise `status: 'error'` with an empty entry, so the renderer is never handed a module URL that cannot open.

Lifecycle-hook failures are contained to one plugin: a synchronous throw from `ready()` removes the instance from the live map, a throw from `dispose()` is caught and warned while the plugin still leaves the live map, and kernel teardown unloads every remaining instance behind a `stopped` guard so the dispose hook runs exactly once per instance.

The directory watchdog creates each plugin root with `fs.mkdirSync(dir, { recursive: true })` before `fs.watch(dir, { recursive: true })` because the install location not existing yet is the normal first-run case; it merges event storms through a settle window (default 300 ms) before invoking the rescan callback once, skips roots it cannot create or watch (explicit `rescan()` remains the fallback), and returns a closer that clears the pending timer and closes every watcher.

`plugins/changed` exists so hot-plugging is visible without waiting for the 1 Hz snapshot: it is emitted on the cordis context by `rescan()`, declared both in the cordis `Events` augmentation and in `BridgeEvents`, forwarded by `FORWARDED_EVENTS` over the `deck:bridge-event` channel, and applied by the page against its last snapshot instead of waiting for the next tick.

Plugin assets are delivered by the privileged `deck-plugin://` scheme rather than a preload API: `registerPluginScheme()` runs at module top level before app ready with `standard`, `secure`, `supportFetchAPI`, `corsEnabled` and `stream` privileges, the panel page itself loads from `deck-plugin://app/index.html` so page and plugin modules share the scheme and ESM semantics, and `installPluginProtocol()` is wired after the kernel starts but before the window loads the page.

The protocol handler rebuilds its asset roots on every request from the app root plus `host.allDirs()` — the live instance map — so a plugin's files become addressable as soon as it is installed and stop resolving once it is removed, an unregistered host is a 404, and successful responses add `access-control-allow-origin: *` for cross-host module loads plus `cache-control: no-store`.

`resolveAssetUrl` is pure (no Electron import) and returns null, which the handler turns into a 404, for a wrong scheme, an unregistered host, malformed percent-encoding, a NUL or backslash in the path, a resolved path outside the asset root, a directory target, a missing file, and any extension outside the delivery whitelist; `../`, `%2e%2e/`, deep `../` chains, backslash traversal and `%00` escape attempts are all pinned by test cases.

Delivery is gated by a MIME whitelist rather than a header nicety: `.js`/`.mjs` must be sent as `text/javascript` or the module is refused, only `.css`, `.json`, `.html`, `.svg`, `.png` and `.woff2` join them, and an unlisted extension is never served at all.

`deck-plugin` is a non-special URL scheme, so host names are matched literally and not case-folded: `deck-plugin://CLOCK/card.js` resolves to nothing while `deck-plugin://clock/card.js` resolves, which lines up with the lowercase-only manifest id charset instead of guessing a mapping.

All plugin file reads happen in the main process's protocol handler; the renderer window keeps `contextIsolation: true`, `sandbox: true` and `nodeIntegration: false` and its only privileged surface is the preload IPC forwarder, and a source-level guard in the kernel contract suite asserts the renderer plugin runtime contains no `require(`/`node:fs` and the preload no `readFileSync`.

Capability trimming narrows data, not privileges: the plugin module is dynamically imported into the panel page's own realm, so it can reach `window.deck` and the DOM directly and its network access is the page's; the capability list is a contract about which snapshot sections the host hands over, not a sandbox for untrusted code.

Because a relative specifier inside a plugin module resolves against that plugin's own `deck-plugin://<id>/` host root, files outside the plugin directory cannot be reached by relative import (the real-machine failure that killed the first five-card run), so the shared presentational helpers `pad`, `pad3`, `pct` and `esc` are handed to plugins through `PluginHost.util` and plugins stay single-file with zero relative imports — while a sub-directory inside the plugin directory remains legitimately addressable.

The renderer runtime keeps three maps — `mounted` (live components with their API, container, trimmed view, view key and entry URL), a per-plugin `generations` token counter, and a `failed` ledger — where unmounting bumps the plugin's own generation so an in-flight import that finishes later is discarded instead of resurrecting a removed component, and the counter is per plugin because a single global counter let concurrently importing cards invalidate each other.

Import and mount failures are recorded per id together with the entry URL and reported as `plugin-load-failed`/`plugin-mount-failed`; no retry happens inside the `FAIL_RETRY_MS` cooldown (30 s) so a 404 card cannot flood the evidence log, a changed entry URL (new revision) or the elapsed cooldown grants one self-healing retry, and a successful mount clears the record.

`syncPlugins` is idempotent and runs on every snapshot and every `plugins/changed`: entries that are no longer `status: 'ok'` are unmounted, a changed entry URL forces unmount plus remount to bypass the ESM module cache, a changed trimmed-view JSON calls `update`, and an unchanged view produces no DOM work at all.

`viewFor` copies only the declared capability sections that also exist as snapshot sections, so a plugin receives a `Partial<PanelSnapshot>` in which undeclared or unavailable sections are absent keys rather than empty values; `mount` receives that first view, `update` fires only when the trimmed view actually changes, and `unmount` runs on removal.

Plugin mounting affects the panel's click-through model: `deps.onDomChanged` is `declareHotZones`, which collects elements carrying the shared `card` class, so a component must put that class (and an id) on its own element inside the host container to become clickable — otherwise it renders into a mouse pass-through region; the acceptance battery asserts both the built-in hotzones and a freshly installed plugin's card rectangle.

Built-in cards are ordinary plugins that live in the build output: sources are `src/renderer/cards/<id>/card.ts` plus a `plugin.json`, `tsc -p tsconfig.renderer.json` compiles the entry and `scripts/copy-assets.mjs` copies each manifest into `dist/renderer/cards/<id>/` while skipping directories without one, and the built-in root `dist/renderer/cards` is scanned first and is also inside the app asset tree even though each card is its own protocol host.

Adding a plugin-visible data capability is a four-step recipe — add the section to `PanelSnapshot`, register the same name in `PLUGIN_CAPABILITIES`, have the owning service fill it in `BridgeService.snapshot()`, and declare it in a manifest — and skipping a step fails silently because the type checker passes while plugins never see the data; narrowing the vocabulary is the same seam, with unknown capability strings dropped silently as the retired `qoder` capability shows.

The plugin install location is `userData/plugins` unless `config.plugins.dir` overrides it: the config module stays Electron-free and its shipped default is an empty string meaning "use the default", which the main process resolves through `userDataPath`, and a non-object `plugins` section or non-string `dir` warns and reverts to the default instead of failing the boot.

`samples/hello-plugin` is the reference third-party plugin: one directory holding a `plugin.json` (id `hello`, `capabilities: ["clock"]`, order 900) and a single-file `card.js` whose default export implements `mount`/`update`/`unmount`, draws into `host.el`, reads only `host.view.clock` and reports `hello-mounted` so the acceptance battery can prove the plugin module itself ran, separately from the host's `plugin-mounted` event.

Plugin id lookups are Map-based throughout the host and the protocol, so prototype-key ids such as `constructor` are addressable and `dirOf`/asset resolution for an unregistered id such as `toString` returns undefined instead of hitting `Object.prototype` — the defence is the data structure, not a banned-name list.

Offline coverage is three plugin suites (`manifest`, `assets`, `service`) plus a plugin section in the kernel contract suite; the renderer runtime and the Electron protocol wiring have no unit tests and are instead covered by the real-machine acceptance battery, whose P11 segment installs the sample plugin at runtime and asserts mount, hotzone presence, reload after editing `card.js`, disappearance on uninstall and recovery on reinstall while the boot evidence count stays unchanged.
